blocks.html: You know from Pressure that pressure is force spread over area, $P = F/A$, measured in pascals ($1\,\text{Pa} = 1\,\text{N/m}^2$), and from Density that density is mass per volume, $\rho = m/V$. Put the two together and you can find the pressure anywhere in a still liquid. It is why your ears hurt at the bottom of a pool and why a dam is thickest at its base.

Picture a column of water inside the lake, with cross-section $A$, reaching from the surface down to depth $h$. It is at rest, so by the first law the forces on it balance. The water below pushes it up with $PA$. The air above pushes it down with $P_0 A$, and its own weight pulls it down with $mg = \rho (Ah) g$. So $PA = P_0 A + \rho A h g$. Divide by $A$: $$P = P_0 + \rho g h.$$ The area cancelled. Only the depth matters, not how wide the water is.

In a still fluid, $P = P_0 + \rho g h$, where $P_0$ is the pressure at the surface (usually the air, about $1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}$) and $h$ is the depth. The gauge pressure $P - P_0 = \rho g h$ leaves out the air. Pressure depends on depth, not on the shape of the container.

So a diver at about $10\,\text{m}$ feels twice the surface pressure, and each further $10\,\text{m}$ adds about one more atmosphere.

blocks.q: A wide tank with a floor of $1.5\,\text{m}^2$ and a thin pipe with a floor of $0.010\,\text{m}^2$ are both filled with water to $2.0\,\text{m}$. Compare the gauge pressure and the force of the water on each floor.
steps: Pressure: both floors are $2.0\,\text{m}$ deep, so both feel $\rho g h = (1000)(9.8)(2.0) = 19{,}600\,\text{Pa}$.

Force on the pipe's floor: $(19{,}600\,\text{Pa})(0.010\,\text{m}^2) = 196\,\text{N}$. Same pressure, very different forces, because the areas differ.

blocks.html: Thinking a wider container, or one holding more water, has more pressure at the bottom. Pressure is force per area: the extra water in a wide tank rests on extra floor. In a container that flares out at the top, the slanted walls hold up the extra water; in one that narrows at the top, the walls push down on the water. Check: the formula $P = P_0 + \rho g h$ has no width in it. A second slip is mixing up gauge and absolute pressure; ask whether the air is included.

blocks.html: In Pressure and Depth you found $P = P_0 + \rho g h$ at every point of a still liquid. Now press on the liquid's surface with a piston, raising $P_0$. What happens to the pressure down below?

Every point's pressure is $P_0$ plus its own $\rho g h$. Pushing on the piston raises $P_0$ by some amount $\Delta P$, and a liquid barely compresses, so the depths and the $\rho g h$ terms stay the same. Then every point's pressure rises by exactly $\Delta P$. That is Pascal's principle: a pressure change in an enclosed fluid reaches every part of it, undiminished.

In a hydraulic system the pressure is the same on both pistons: $\dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{F_2}{A_2}$, so $F_2 = F_1 \dfrac{A_2}{A_1}$. The liquid's volume is fixed, so $A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2$: the big piston moves a shorter distance. Work in equals work out, $F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2$.

blocks.title: A car lift
blocks.q: A car lift's large piston has an area of $0.50\,\text{m}^2$ and its small piston $0.010\,\text{m}^2$. What force on the small piston holds up a $1500\,\text{kg}$ car?
steps: The large piston must push up with the car's weight: $F_2 = mg = (1500\,\text{kg})(9.8\,\text{m/s}^2) = 14{,}700\,\text{N}$.
$F_1 = 294\,\text{N}$, about the weight of a $30\,\text{kg}$ child.

blocks.title: Where the work goes
blocks.q: In the same lift you push the small piston down $25\,\text{cm}$. How far does the car rise, and how do the two works compare?
steps: Volume moved: $A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2$, so $d_2 = d_1 \dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = (25\,\text{cm})\dfrac{0.010}{0.50} = 0.50\,\text{cm}$.
Work out: $F_2 d_2 = (14{,}700\,\text{N})(0.0050\,\text{m}) = 73.5\,\text{J}$. Equal, as work and energy conservation demand.

blocks.title: Round pistons
blocks.q: A press has round pistons with diameters $2.0\,\text{cm}$ and $10\,\text{cm}$. By what factor does it multiply force?
steps: The force grows by the area ratio, and a circle's area is $\pi d^2/4$.
Five times the diameter gives twenty-five times the force.

blocks.html: Thinking a hydraulic lift gives you energy for free. It multiplies force, not energy: to lift the car $1\,\text{cm}$ with $\tfrac{1}{50}$ of its weight, you must push $50\,\text{cm}$. Check any machine by comparing $F d$ on the way in and on the way out; without friction they are equal, and with friction the output is less.
Car brakes, excavator arms and barber chairs all use Pascal's principle: a liquid in a closed line carries a pressure change from where it is made to where it is needed.

blocks.html: A rock feels lighter under water, and a steel ship floats. Both come from pressure growing with depth: the water pushes harder on the bottom of an object than on its top.

Take a box of height $L$ and top area $A$, held under water with its top at depth $h$. The water pushes down on the top with $(P_0 + \rho g h)A$ and up on the bottom with $(P_0 + \rho g (h + L))A$. The side pushes cancel. The net push is up: $$F_b = \rho g L A = \rho_{\text{fluid}} V g,$$ the weight of the fluid that would fill the box's space. Another way to see it: replace the box with water. That water would float in place, so the surrounding water must push up on it with exactly its weight. The surrounding water cannot tell what fills the space.

Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid pushed aside, $F_b = \rho_{\text{fluid}} V_{\text{sub}} g$. An object denser than the fluid sinks; a less dense one floats with the fraction $\rho_{\text{object}}/\rho_{\text{fluid}}$ of its volume under the surface.

blocks.q: A $1.0\,\text{L}$ ($0.0010\,\text{m}^3$) aluminum block ($2700\,\text{kg/m}^3$) hangs from a spring scale, fully under fresh water. What does the scale read?
steps: Buoyant force: $F_b = \rho_{\text{water}} V g = (1000)(0.0010)(9.8) = 9.8\,\text{N}$, the weight of one liter of water.
Forces balance: scale + buoyant force = weight, so the scale reads $26.5 - 9.8 = 16.7\,\text{N}$.

blocks.title: The tip of the iceberg
blocks.q: Ice ($917\,\text{kg/m}^3$) floats in seawater ($1025\,\text{kg/m}^3$). What fraction of an iceberg is under the surface?
steps: Floating, the buoyant force equals the weight: $\rho_{\text{sea}} V_{\text{sub}} g = \rho_{\text{ice}} V g$.
About $89\%$ is under water; only about a tenth shows.

steps: The buoyant force is the lost weight: $30.0 - 27.0 = 3.0\,\text{N}$.
$\rho = m/V = 10{,}000\,\text{kg/m}^3$, ten times water, since it lost a tenth of its weight.

blocks.html: Thinking the buoyant force depends on the object's own weight or density. It depends only on the volume under the surface and the fluid's density. An aluminum block and a lead block of the same size feel the same buoyant force; the lead sinks because its weight is bigger, not because the water pushes less. Check: $F_b = \rho_{\text{fluid}} V_{\text{sub}} g$ has nothing about the object in it except its submerged volume.

blocks.html: Put your thumb over the end of a garden hose and the water shoots out faster. Nothing new pushed it; the water simply had to get through a smaller opening. This lesson turns that into a rule, using the pressure picture of a liquid and a proportion.

A liquid barely compresses. In a pipe that is full, water cannot pile up anywhere, so every second the same volume must pass every cross-section. In a time $\Delta t$ the water moves a distance $v\,\Delta t$, so the volume passing is $A v\,\Delta t$, and the volume per second is $$Q = Av.$$ If $Q$ is the same at two places, then $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$. Halve the area and the speed must double.
Flow rate $Q = Av$ (in $\text{m}^3\text{/s}$; $1\,\text{L} = 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$). For a liquid filling a pipe, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$: the liquid moves fastest where the pipe is narrowest.

blocks.q: A round pipe narrows from a diameter of $4.0\,\text{cm}$ to $2.0\,\text{cm}$. Water moves at $0.50\,\text{m/s}$ in the wide part. How fast in the narrow part?
steps: Area goes as diameter squared ($A = \pi d^2/4$), so $\dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \left(\dfrac{4.0}{2.0}\right)^2 = 4$.
$v_2 = (0.50\,\text{m/s})(4) = 2.0\,\text{m/s}$. Half the diameter means four times the speed.

blocks.html: Thinking water slows down where a pipe narrows, as if it were squeezed or held back. In a full pipe it must speed up, or the water behind it would have nowhere to go. Rivers show it too: the same water that drifts through a wide, deep pool races through narrow rapids. Check: does $A \times v$ come out the same at both places?
Air compresses, so $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ holds for a gas only when its density stays about the same, as in slow airflow.

blocks.html: In Flow Rate and Continuity water sped up in a narrow pipe. But speeding up takes a net force. Something must push the water from behind harder than the water ahead pushes back, so the pressure must drop where the water is fast. Bernoulli's equation makes this exact, using conservation of energy.

Follow a small parcel of water of volume $\Delta V$ (mass $\rho\,\Delta V$) from point 1 to point 2 in steady flow. The water behind pushes it forward and does work $P_1 \Delta V$; the water ahead pushes back and takes away $P_2 \Delta V$. With no friction, this net work changes the parcel's kinetic and gravitational energy: $$(P_1 - P_2)\Delta V = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho \Delta V (v_2^2 - v_1^2) + \rho \Delta V g (h_2 - h_1).$$ Divide by $\Delta V$ and gather each point's terms on its own side. For still water ($v_1 = v_2 = 0$) it gives back $P_2 = P_1 + \rho g (h_1 - h_2)$, the rule from Pressure and Depth.

Bernoulli's equation: along a streamline of steady, frictionless flow of a liquid, $$P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}.$$ Each term is energy per cubic meter. At the same height, faster fluid has lower pressure; at the same speed, higher fluid has lower pressure.

blocks.q: A large open tank has a small hole $1.8\,\text{m}$ below the water surface. How fast does the water squirt out?

Bernoulli leaves $\rho g h = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2$, so $v_2 = \sqrt{2gh}$.
$v_2 = \sqrt{2(9.8)(1.8)} = \sqrt{35.3} = 5.94\,\text{m/s}$, as fast as a stone dropped $1.8\,\text{m}$.

blocks.html: Thinking faster fluid pushes harder, so its pressure must be higher. A fast jet does push hard on whatever stops it, but that is the force of stopping its momentum. Inside the moving stream, sideways pressure is lower where it moves faster. Check with forces: water speeds up only if the pressure behind it is higher than the pressure ahead.

Bernoulli's equation leaves out friction (viscosity) and assumes the liquid's density stays fixed. Real pipes lose some pressure to friction, so it gives an upper limit for speeds and a lower limit for pressure drops.

blocks.html: In Kinetic Molecular Theory you met a gas as a swarm of tiny molecules flying in all directions, with pressure coming from their hits on the walls. Here that picture becomes one equation that ties together pressure $P$, volume $V$, temperature $T$ and the amount of gas. You will rearrange it often, as in Solving for a Variable.

Think about the hits on the walls. Twice as many molecules make twice as many hits, so $P \propto n$. Hotter molecules move faster, so they hit harder and more often, and the pressure grows in proportion to the absolute temperature. Give the same molecules twice the volume, and their hits spread over more wall and come less often, so $P \propto 1/V$. Put together, $P \propto nT/V$. The constant that makes it an equation is the gas constant $R$. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, where this pressure would drop to zero; that is why the law needs kelvins.

$$PV = nRT = Nk_BT$$ with $P$ in pascals, $V$ in cubic meters, $T$ in kelvins ($T = T_C + 273$), $n$ in moles, $N$ the number of molecules, $R = 8.31\,\text{J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$ and $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{J/K}$.

blocks.html: Using Celsius. Warming a gas from $20\,^\circ\text{C}$ to $40\,^\circ\text{C}$ does not double its pressure, because $40\,^\circ\text{C}$ is not twice as hot as $20\,^\circ\text{C}$: it is $313\,\text{K}$ against $293\,\text{K}$. Check: convert every temperature to kelvins before it goes into the gas law, and remember that a temperature of $0\,^\circ\text{C}$ would make $P = 0$ if Celsius were allowed.
Real gases follow $PV = nRT$ closely at everyday pressures and temperatures. It fails near the point where a gas condenses into a liquid, when the molecules' own size and attraction start to matter.

blocks.html: The ideal gas law says what a gas does. Kinetic theory explains why, from Newton's laws applied to the molecules. The payoff is a surprising fact: temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

Put $N$ molecules of mass $m$ in a cube of side $L$. One molecule with $x$-velocity $v_x$ bounces off the right wall, and its momentum changes by $2mv_x$. It returns every $2L/v_x$ seconds, so its average force on that wall is $\dfrac{2mv_x}{2L/v_x} = \dfrac{mv_x^2}{L}$. For all $N$ molecules, divide by the wall's area $L^2$: $P = \dfrac{Nm\overline{v_x^2}}{L^3}$. The motion is random in three directions, so $\overline{v_x^2} = \tfrac{1}{3}\overline{v^2}$, and $$PV = \tfrac{1}{3}Nm\overline{v^2} = \tfrac{2}{3}N\left(\tfrac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2}\right).$$ Compare $PV = Nk_BT$: the average kinetic energy of a molecule is $\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$.

$\bar K = \tfrac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$, the same for every gas at the same temperature. The rms speed is $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3k_BT}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$ ($M$ in kg/mol). A monatomic ideal gas stores $U = \tfrac{3}{2}nRT$.

blocks.html: Thinking every molecule moves at the same speed, or that heavier molecules at the same temperature carry more kinetic energy. Speeds spread out widely (the histogram), and $v_{\text{rms}}$ is only a typical value. At one temperature every kind of molecule has the same average kinetic energy; a heavy molecule pays for its mass by moving more slowly. Check: in $\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$ there is no mass.

Molecules with two or more atoms can also spin, which stores extra energy. So $U = \tfrac{3}{2}nRT$ is for monatomic gases such as helium, neon and argon; air near room temperature stores about $\tfrac{5}{2}nRT$.

blocks.html: In Calorimetry you used $Q = mc\Delta T$ to find the heat that warms an object. But heat a pot of ice and the thermometer stalls at $0\,^\circ\text{C}$, and again at $100\,^\circ\text{C}$, as you saw in Changes of State. Where does the heat go while the temperature stands still?

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules. During melting, the heat goes into pulling molecules out of the crystal's fixed places, raising their potential energy instead of their speed. So the temperature stays put until every bit of ice has melted. Boiling pulls the molecules completely apart, which takes far more energy, so $L_v$ is much bigger than $L_f$.

Changing the state of a mass $m$ at its melting or boiling point takes $Q = mL$, with no change in temperature. For water, $L_f = 3.34 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J/kg}$ and $L_v = 2.26 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J/kg}$. For a whole heating job, add the heat of every stage.

blocks.html: You met conduction in Conduction, Convection and Radiation: heat passing through a material from molecule to molecule. Now we ask how fast. Builders, cooks and engineers all need the rate, in joules per second, or watts, and often need to solve the formula for a thickness or an area.

Think of heat crossing a slab of thickness $L$ and area $A$. Twice the area is like two slabs side by side, so twice the rate: $P \propto A$. A bigger temperature difference drives heat harder: $P \propto \Delta T$. A thicker slab spreads the same temperature difference over more distance, so each layer passes on less: $P \propto 1/L$. What is left is the material, through its thermal conductivity $k$. In metals, free electrons carry energy quickly, so $k$ is large; in foam, trapped air carries it slowly.
$$P = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{kA\,\Delta T}{L}$$ Thin, wide slabs with big temperature differences pass heat fastest. A temperature difference in $^\circ\text{C}$ is the same number in kelvins.

blocks.html: The Sun warms your face across $150$ million kilometers of empty space. That is radiation, the one kind of heat transfer that needs no material. It carries energy as electromagnetic waves, mostly the infrared part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

The charged particles in every object jiggle with thermal motion, and moving charges give off electromagnetic waves. Hotter means more vigorous jiggling, so more power comes out, and more of it at high frequencies (short wavelengths). Measurements, explained by Planck's theory, give two simple laws. The total power grows as the fourth power of the kelvin temperature, and the wavelength of the peak shrinks in proportion to $1/T$. Good absorbers are also good emitters; the emissivity $e$, from 0 to 1, measures both.

Stefan–Boltzmann: $P = e\sigma AT^4$, with $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K}^4)$ and $T$ in kelvins. An object in surroundings at $T_{\text{env}}$ loses net power $e\sigma A(T^4 - T_{\text{env}}^4)$. Wien: $\lambda_{\max}T = 2.898 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\cdot\text{K}$.

blocks.title: Double the temperature
blocks.q: A hot plate at $27\,^\circ\text{C}$ is heated to $327\,^\circ\text{C}$. By what factor does its radiated power grow?
steps: Kelvins: $27 + 273 = 300\,\text{K}$ and $327 + 273 = 600\,\text{K}$, so the temperature doubled.
Not $2$, and not $(327/27)^4 \approx 21{,}500$ from Celsius numbers.

blocks.title: Peak wavelengths
blocks.q: Where do the Sun's surface ($5772\,\text{K}$) and your skin ($306\,\text{K}$) radiate most strongly?
steps: Sun: $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{2.898 \times 10^{-3}}{5772}\,\text{m} = 5.02 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 502\,\text{nm}$, blue-green light in the middle of the visible range.
Skin: $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{2.898 \times 10^{-3}}{306}\,\text{m} = 9.47 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}$, about $9.5\,\mu\text{m}$, in the infrared. Thermal cameras see it.

blocks.title: Losing heat in a room
blocks.q: A person with $1.5\,\text{m}^2$ of skin at $306\,\text{K}$ ($e = 0.97$) stands in a room at $293\,\text{K}$. What is the net power lost by radiation?
steps: $P = (0.97)(5.67 \times 10^{-8})(1.5)(1.398 \times 10^{9}) = 115\,\text{W}$, about as much as a resting body produces. Clothing cuts this loss by keeping the outer surface cooler.

blocks.html: Thinking only glowing objects radiate, or that doubling the temperature doubles the power. Everything above absolute zero radiates; cool things just radiate in the infrared, which we cannot see. And the power goes as $T^4$: doubling the kelvin temperature multiplies it by $16$. Check: are your temperatures in kelvins, and did you raise them to the fourth power before subtracting?

blocks.html: A gas can push a piston, so it can do work. In Work as Area Under a Force Graph work was the area under a force–distance graph. For a gas, the same idea becomes the area under a pressure–volume graph, using the gas law to connect the states.

A gas at pressure $P$ pushes on a piston of area $A$ with force $PA$. If the piston moves out a small distance $\Delta x$, the gas does work $PA\,\Delta x = P\,\Delta V$ on it. That energy leaves the gas, so the work done on the gas is $W = -P\,\Delta V$. If the pressure changes as the volume changes, add up thin strips: the size of the work is the area under the path on the P–V diagram.

Work done on a gas: $W = -P\Delta V$ at constant pressure; in general $|W|$ is the area under the path on a P–V diagram. Expansion: $W < 0$ (the gas does work). Compression: $W > 0$. Constant volume: $W = 0$. Handy: $1\,\text{kPa} \cdot \text{L} = 1\,\text{J}$.

blocks.html: Energy is conserved, and for a gas there are two ways for it to cross the boundary: heat $Q$, which flows because of a temperature difference, and work $W$, a force acting through a distance, which you met in Work Done on a Gas. What arrives is stored as internal energy $U$, the energy of the molecules' motion, which for a monatomic gas is $\tfrac{3}{2}nRT$ from Temperature and Molecular Energy.

Treat the gas like a bank account. Deposits are heat flowing in and work done on the gas; withdrawals are heat flowing out and work the gas does. The balance can change only by the deposits minus the withdrawals. Written with signs, that is the first law. It is conservation of energy, nothing more, but it lets heat and work trade places: a gas can take in heat and spend it all as work, so its temperature need not rise.

$$\Delta U = Q + W$$ $Q > 0$ when heat flows into the gas; $W > 0$ when work is done on the gas ($W = -P\Delta V$). For an ideal gas, $U$ depends only on $T$: $\Delta U = 0$ whenever the temperature ends where it started.

blocks.html: The first law $\Delta U = Q + W$ holds for every process, but it has three unknowns. Real processes are often simple enough to fix one of them: the volume, the pressure, the temperature, or the heat. Each choice decides how the energy splits.

For a monatomic ideal gas, $U = \tfrac{3}{2}nRT = \tfrac{3}{2}PV$. Hold $V$ fixed and no work is done, so all heat becomes internal energy. Hold $T$ fixed and $U$ cannot change, so $Q = -W$: heat must flow in to pay for the work. Allow no heat (insulate the gas, or act too fast for heat to flow) and $\Delta U = W$: work done on the gas heats it, and a gas that does work cools. Hold $P$ fixed and both happen: heat raises $U$ and pays for the work.

blocks.html: An engine cannot expand forever; it must come back to where it started and go again. A path on the P–V diagram that returns to its starting state is a cycle. Using the processes you know, we can do the bookkeeping for a whole cycle.

Internal energy belongs to the state. Back at the starting $P$ and $V$, the gas is back at its starting $T$ and $U$, so $\Delta U = 0$ around any cycle. Then the first law gives $Q_{\text{net}} = -W_{\text{net}}$: the net heat that flows in equals the net work the gas does. The gas does positive work while it expands and negative work while it is compressed; if it expands at a higher pressure than it is compressed at, the difference is the area inside the loop.

Around a cycle, $\Delta U = 0$ and $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{by}}$. The net work done by the gas equals the area enclosed: positive for a clockwise cycle (an engine), negative for a counterclockwise one (a refrigerator).

blocks.html: A car engine, a power plant's turbine and a steam locomotive all do one thing: take heat from something hot, turn part of it into work, and let the rest go. Each runs the kind of cycle you just learned, and its efficiency is what you get out over what you put in.

Around a cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so energy in equals energy out: $Q_H = W + Q_C$. Why can't $Q_C$ be zero? To return to its start, the gas must be compressed again. Compressing it while it is hot would cost all the work it just did, so the engine cools it first, and cooling means giving heat $Q_C$ to something colder. This is the second law of thermodynamics: no engine running in a cycle can turn heat completely into work.
$$e = \frac{W}{Q_H} = 1 - \frac{Q_C}{Q_H}, \qquad Q_H = W + Q_C$$ Every heat engine gives off some heat, so $e < 1$.

blocks.html: Every heat engine wastes some heat. How little? In 1824 Sadi Carnot found the answer: the limit depends only on the temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs.

Carnot imagined an engine with no friction, which takes in heat only at $T_H$, gives it off only at $T_C$, and could run backward as easily as forward. For it, $\dfrac{Q_C}{Q_H} = \dfrac{T_C}{T_H}$ with kelvin temperatures, so $e = 1 - T_C/T_H$. No real engine can do better. If one could, you could use it to drive Carnot's engine backward as a refrigerator, and the pair would carry heat from cold to hot with no outside work, which never happens.
$$e_{\max} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} \quad \text{(kelvins!)}$$ A hotter source or a colder sink raises the limit. Real engines fall below it.

blocks.html: The formula shows the two ways to build a better engine: make the hot side hotter or the cold side colder. That is why power plants run their steam as hot as their materials allow. The cold side is usually the air or a river, so it cannot go much below about $280\,\text{K}$, and absolute zero itself can never be reached, so no engine can ever reach $100\%$.

blocks.html: Heat flows from hot to cold on its own. A refrigerator moves it the other way, from the cold food to the warm kitchen. It is a heat engine run backward: work goes in, and heat is pumped uphill.

Over each cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so energy in equals energy out: the heat $Q_C$ taken from the cold side plus the work $W$ equals the heat $Q_H$ given to the hot side. A refrigerator is rated by how much heat it removes per joule of work. A heat pump, the same machine pointed at a house, is rated by how much heat it delivers per joule, and that is always more than one joule, because it also brings in the heat it collected from outside.

$$Q_H = Q_C + W, \qquad \text{COP}_{\text{fridge}} = \frac{Q_C}{W}, \qquad \text{COP}_{\text{heat pump}} = \frac{Q_H}{W}$$ The best possible (Carnot) values are $\dfrac{T_C}{T_H - T_C}$ and $\dfrac{T_H}{T_H - T_C}$, with kelvins.

blocks.html: Why does heat flow from hot to cold and never the other way on its own? Why can't the Carnot limit be beaten? One quantity answers both: entropy.

Define the entropy change of something that takes in heat $Q$ at a steady kelvin temperature $T$ as $\Delta S = Q/T$. Now let heat $Q$ flow from a hot reservoir to a cold one. The hot one loses $Q/T_H$, the cold one gains $Q/T_C$, and since $T_C < T_H$ the gain is bigger: the total goes up. Heat flowing from cold to hot would make the total go down, and that is exactly what never happens by itself. At the level of molecules, entropy counts the ways to arrange the energy; spread-out energy has far more arrangements, so it is overwhelmingly likely.

$\Delta S = \dfrac{Q}{T}$ for heat $Q$ at kelvin temperature $T$. Second law: the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. It rises in every real process and stays the same only in an ideal, reversible one.

blocks.html: Thinking entropy can never go down anywhere. It can go down in one part of a system, such as the food in a refrigerator or water freezing into ice, as long as the entropy of the surroundings rises by more. The second law is about the total for an isolated system. Check: list every object that exchanges heat, and add up their $Q/T$ values.
For Carnot's ideal engine the total is exactly zero: $Q_H/T_H = Q_C/T_C$, which gives its efficiency $1 - T_C/T_H$. Any real engine adds entropy, so it gives off more heat and does less work.

blocks.html: In Attraction and Repulsion you saw that like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Now we look at charge itself: where it comes from, how objects get it, and the two rules it always obeys.

Ordinary matter is made of atoms: protons, each with charge $+e$, and electrons, each with $-e$, where $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. A neutral object is not empty of charge; it holds equal numbers of both. Charging an object never creates charge: it moves electrons from one place to another. So the total charge never changes (conservation), and any object's net charge is a whole number of electrons' worth, $q = \pm Ne$ (quantization).

Charge is conserved and comes in whole multiples of $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. Objects charge by friction (rubbing moves electrons), by contact (a conductor shares charge), or by induction (a nearby charge pushes charges around, and a ground connection lets some leave or arrive).

items: Conductors, such as metals, have electrons free to move through them, so charge spreads over them.
Insulators, such as plastic and glass, hold their electrons in place, so charge stays where it is put.
Two identical metal spheres that touch end up sharing their total charge equally.

blocks.html: Thinking a neutral object holds no charges at all, so nothing could attract it. A neutral object has equal amounts of positive and negative charge, and they can shift. That is why a charged balloon picks up neutral bits of paper: the paper polarizes, and its near side, with the opposite charge, is attracted more strongly than its far side is repelled.

blocks.html: How strongly do two charges push or pull? In 1785 Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured it with a delicate twisting balance. The answer looks just like Newton's law of gravitation, with charges in place of masses. It builds on the charges you just met.

The force between two point charges grows in proportion to each charge and falls off as the square of the distance. The inverse square has a picture behind it: the influence of a charge spreads out over spheres whose area grows as $4\pi r^2$, so at twice the distance it is spread over four times the area. Unlike gravity, charge comes in two signs, so the force can push as well as pull. And it is enormously stronger: between an electron and a proton the electric force is about $10^{39}$ times the gravitational one.

$$F = k\frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}, \quad k = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$$ The force acts along the line between the charges: like charges repel, unlike attract. Each charge feels the same size of force (Newton's third law).

blocks.html: With three or more charges, each pair still obeys Coulomb's law, and the force from one charge does not change because others are nearby. So the net force is the sum of the separate forces, added as vectors, the way you learned in Adding Vectors by Components.

This is the superposition principle, and it is an experimental fact: the force between two charges is the same whether or not other charges are around. So you can find each force on its own and then add. Forces are vectors, so they add tip to tail. On a line, that means adding with signs; at an angle, it means adding components.

$\vec F_{\text{net}} = \vec F_1 + \vec F_2 + \cdots$, each from Coulomb's law. Find each force's size, decide its direction (toward or away from the charge that makes it), then add components: $F_x = \sum F_{ix}$, $F_y = \sum F_{iy}$, $F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$.

blocks.html: How does one charge push another across empty space? In Fields: Forces at a Distance you met the idea of a field. Here we make it precise for electric charges, starting from Coulomb's law.

A charge $Q$ changes the space around it, and any other charge placed there feels a force. To describe that change without naming the second charge, place a small test charge $q$ at a point and divide the force on it by $q$. Since the force is proportional to $q$, the ratio is the same for any test charge: it belongs to the point, not to the test charge. For a point charge, Coulomb's law gives $F = k|Qq|/r^2$, so $E = F/q = k|Q|/r^2$.

$\vec E = \vec F/q$, the force per coulomb, in $\text{N/C}$. A point charge makes $E = k\dfrac{|Q|}{r^2}$, pointing away from a positive charge and toward a negative one. A charge $q$ in a field feels $\vec F = q\vec E$: along $\vec E$ if $q > 0$, opposite if $q < 0$.

blocks.html: With several charges, each one makes its own field, and the field at a point is their vector sum, for the same reason that forces add. Field lines then let you see the whole pattern at a glance.

The force on a test charge is the vector sum of the forces from each charge. Divide every force by the test charge and the same sum holds for fields: $\vec E = \vec E_1 + \vec E_2 + \cdots$. Field lines are drawn so that at every point they run along $\vec E$, and so that they crowd together where $E$ is strong. Since the field has only one direction at each point, two lines can never cross.

Add the field vectors from each charge. Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones, point along $\vec E$, are closer where the field is stronger, and never cross. They show the direction of the force, not the path a charge must follow.

blocks.html: Between two large, flat, oppositely charged plates, the electric field is the same everywhere: the same size and the same direction. A charge there feels a constant force, so it moves just like a ball in projectile motion, with the electric force playing the part of gravity.

Each plate is a sheet of charge whose field does not weaken with distance (for points close to a large sheet). Between the plates the two fields point the same way and add; outside they point opposite ways and cancel. So the field is uniform between the plates and nearly zero outside. A uniform field gives a constant force $qE$ and a constant acceleration $a = qE/m$, and all of constant-acceleration kinematics applies.

In a uniform field, $a = \dfrac{qE}{m}$, constant. A positive charge accelerates along $\vec E$; an electron accelerates opposite to $\vec E$. A charge entering sideways follows a parabola: constant speed along the plates, constant acceleration across them.

blocks.html: Lifting a ball stores gravitational potential energy, and far from Earth it is $U = -GMm/r$. Pushing two charges together, or pulling them apart, stores energy in the same way, with a formula of the same shape, built on Coulomb's law.

The Coulomb force is conservative, like gravity: the work it does depends only on the start and the end. So there is a potential energy, and choosing $U = 0$ when the charges are far apart gives $$U = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}.$$ The signs of the charges stay in. Like charges repel: you must push to bring them together, and that work is stored, so $U > 0$ and it grows as they get closer. Unlike charges attract: they release energy as they come together, so $U < 0$, the same as gravity's $-GMm/r$.
$U = k\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r}$, with signs, and $U = 0$ far apart. For several charges, add $U$ for every pair. With only electric forces acting, $K + U$ stays constant.

blocks.html: The potential energy of a charge depends on that charge. Divide it out, just as we did to get the electric field from the force, and you get a property of the place itself: the electric potential, measured in volts.

If a charge $q$ at some point has potential energy $U$, then $V = U/q$ is the energy each coulomb would have there. Near a point charge, $U = kQq/r$, so $V = kQ/r$. Potential is a scalar, so for several charges you just add numbers, signs included. When a charge moves between two points, its potential energy changes by $q\Delta V$; if only electric forces act, its kinetic energy changes by the opposite amount.

$V = \dfrac{U}{q}$, in volts ($1\,\text{V} = 1\,\text{J/C}$). Near a point charge, $V = k\dfrac{Q}{r}$. A charge crossing a potential difference $\Delta V$ has $\Delta U = q\Delta V$ and $\Delta K = -q\Delta V$. One electron volt, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$, is the energy an electron gains crossing $1\,\text{V}$.

blocks.html: A contour map joins points of equal height; equipotentials join points of equal electric potential. Together with the field lines, they give the complete picture of a field, and they connect the field to the voltage of a battery.

Move a charge along an equipotential: $\Delta V = 0$, so the field does no work, which means the force has no component along the move. So $\vec E$ is always perpendicular to the equipotentials. Move a positive charge along the field and the field does positive work, so its potential energy, and the potential, drop: $\vec E$ points from high to low potential. In a uniform field, the drop over a distance $d$ along the field is $\Delta V = Ed$, so $E = \Delta V/d$ and $1\,\text{V/m} = 1\,\text{N/C}$.

Field lines cross equipotentials at right angles and point toward lower potential. Equipotentials are crowded where the field is strong: $E = \dfrac{\Delta V}{d}$ (exactly so in a uniform field, such as between parallel plates).

blocks.html: A capacitor stores charge: two conductors, usually flat plates, separated by a gap. Connect it to a battery and charge $+Q$ builds on one plate and $-Q$ on the other, with the uniform field you met in Equipotentials and Field Strength between them.

The field between closely spaced plates of area $A$ is $E = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A}$, where $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}$. The voltage across the gap is then $V = Ed = \dfrac{Qd}{\varepsilon_0 A}$. So $Q$ is proportional to $V$, and the ratio $C = Q/V = \varepsilon_0 A/d$ depends only on the shape. Fill the gap with an insulator and its molecules polarize, weakening the field for the same charge by a factor $\kappa$, the dielectric constant, so $C$ grows by $\kappa$.

$$C = \frac{Q}{V}, \qquad C = \frac{\kappa\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$$ Capacitance, in farads ($1\,\text{F} = 1\,\text{C/V}$), depends on the plates' area, their gap and the material between them, not on the charge or the voltage.

blocks.html: A charged capacitor stores energy: a camera flash or a defibrillator dumps it in a fraction of a second. How much? The answer comes from the same idea as work as the area under a graph.

Charge the capacitor a little at a time. When it already holds charge $q$, its voltage is $v = q/C$, and moving the next small bit $\Delta q$ across takes work $v\,\Delta q$. At first $v = 0$ and it costs nothing; near the end each bit costs almost $V$. On a graph of $v$ against $q$, the work is the area under a straight line from $0$ to $(Q, V)$: a triangle with area $\tfrac{1}{2}QV$.
$$U = \tfrac{1}{2}QV = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$$ Use whichever form matches what you know. At fixed $C$, doubling the voltage stores four times the energy.

blocks.html: In Current and Voltage you met current as the flow of charge around a circuit. Now we measure it. Because charge is conserved, counting the charge that passes a point tells you a great deal about the whole circuit.

Stand at one point in a wire and count the charge going past. The current is how much passes per second. In a metal the moving charges are electrons, and they drift slowly, typically well under a millimeter per second, but the push that moves them spreads through the circuit almost at once, so a lamp lights the instant the switch closes. Charge cannot pile up anywhere in a steady circuit, so on a single path the same current passes every point, before and after each part.

$$I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}, \qquad 1\,\text{A} = 1\,\text{C/s}$$ Conventional current points the way positive charge would flow: out of the battery's $+$ terminal, around the circuit, and back into its $-$ terminal. In wires, electrons drift the opposite way.

blocks.html: Ohm's law, $V = IR$, says how much voltage it takes to push a current through a resistance $R$. But what decides $R$? For a wire, three things: what it is made of, how long it is, and how thick it is.

Electrons drifting through a metal keep bumping into its vibrating atoms. A longer wire means more bumps along the way, like more resistors in a row: $R \propto L$. A thicker wire gives the electrons more paths side by side, like more resistors in parallel: $R \propto 1/A$. What is left depends on the material, its resistivity $\rho$. In most metals the atoms vibrate more when hot, so $\rho$ rises with temperature.
$$R = \rho\frac{L}{A}$$ with $\rho$ in $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$, $L$ in meters and $A$ in square meters. For a round wire, $A = \pi r^2 = \pi d^2/4$.

blocks.html: A resistor turns electrical energy into thermal energy: that is how toasters, heaters and old-style light bulbs work. In Electric Power and Energy Use you met $P = IV$. Combined with $V = IR$ and what you know about resistance, it comes in three forms.

Each coulomb that crosses a resistor drops through a potential difference $V$, so it gives up $V$ joules. If $I$ coulombs cross each second, the resistor receives $IV$ joules per second: $P = IV$. Substituting Ohm's law: with $V = IR$, $P = I^2R$; with $I = V/R$, $P = V^2/R$. They are one idea; pick the form that uses what you know.

$$P = IV = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ Same current (series): the bigger resistor uses more power. Same voltage (parallel): the smaller resistor uses more power. Energy $=$ power $\times$ time; $1\,\text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J}$.

blocks.html: In Series and Parallel Circuits you saw that a series circuit has a single path. Now we put numbers on it, using the resistances of its parts.

With one path, every charge passes through every resistor, so the same current $I$ flows through each. Each resistor takes its share of the energy per coulomb, $V_i = IR_i$, and the shares must add up to what the battery gives: $V = IR_1 + IR_2 + IR_3 = I(R_1 + R_2 + R_3)$. The resistors act together like one resistor of $R_1 + R_2 + R_3$, which makes sense: it is like one long wire.

Series: one current through all; the voltages add up to the battery's; $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots$. Each resistor's share is $V_i = IR_i$, so the biggest resistor takes the biggest share of the voltage.

blocks.html: In parallel, each resistor gets its own path between the same two points. That changes everything you just learned about series circuits: now the voltage is shared and the currents add.

Each branch connects directly across the same two points, so each has the same voltage $V$. Each branch's current is $V/R_i$, and at the junction the currents add: $I = \dfrac{V}{R_1} + \dfrac{V}{R_2} + \cdots$. If one resistor $R_{\text{eq}}$ is to draw the same $I$, then $\dfrac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \cdots$. Every extra branch is an extra path, so the total current goes up and $R_{\text{eq}}$ goes down, below even the smallest resistor.

Parallel: same voltage across each branch; the branch currents add; $\dfrac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \cdots$. For two: $R_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$. For $n$ equal resistors: $R/n$.

blocks.html: Real circuits mix series and parallel parts. The plan is to shrink the circuit one step at a time to a single resistor, then work back out to find every current and voltage.

Replacing a group by its equivalent does not change anything outside the group: the rest of the circuit sees the same current for the same voltage. So you may collapse groups one by one. The only care is to collapse a group only if it really is series (same current, no junction in between) or really is parallel (both ends joined to the same two points).

Reduce: combine true series groups ($R_1 + R_2$) and true parallel groups ($\tfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$), innermost first, until one resistor is left; $I = V/R_{\text{eq}}$. Expand: go back step by step, using $V = IR$ on each piece; series pieces share current, parallel pieces share voltage.

blocks.html: Some circuits cannot be reduced to series and parallel groups. For those, two rules from the conservation laws do all the work. The first is about junctions, the points where three or more wires meet, as in the parallel circuits you have seen.

In a steady circuit, charge does not pile up anywhere, and it is never created or destroyed. So every coulomb per second that arrives at a junction must leave it. That is Kirchhoff's junction rule, and it is charge conservation written for currents.

At any junction, $\sum I_{\text{in}} = \sum I_{\text{out}}$. How the current divides depends on the branches: parallel branches share one voltage, so each gets $I_i = V/R_i$, and the smaller resistance gets the larger share.

Gustav Kirchhoff stated this rule and the loop rule in 1845, as a student. When you do not know which way a current flows, guess a direction and draw its arrow; if the answer comes out negative, the current flows the other way, and nothing else needs fixing.

blocks.html: The second rule is about loops, closed paths around a circuit. With the junction rule, it solves any circuit, even ones with several batteries that series-parallel reduction cannot handle. The equations you get are a system, solved by elimination.

Electric potential has one value at each point, like height on a hiking map. Walk around any closed loop and you come back to where you started, at the same potential, so all the rises and drops along the way add to zero. In energy terms: a charge going once around the loop gains from the batteries exactly what it gives to the resistors.

Around any closed loop, $\sum \Delta V = 0$. Through a battery from $-$ to $+$: $+\varepsilon$ (from $+$ to $-$: $-\varepsilon$). Through a resistor in the direction of the current: $-IR$ (against it: $+IR$). Guess the current directions; a negative answer means that current flows the other way.

blocks.html: A real battery is not a perfect source of voltage. The chemistry inside it resists the flow of charge a little, so a battery behaves like an ideal one, its EMF $\varepsilon$, with a small internal resistance $r$ in series. The loop rule shows what that does.

Walk around a loop with the battery and a load $R$: $\varepsilon - Ir - IR = 0$, so $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r}$. The voltage you can measure across the battery's terminals is what is left after the internal drop: $V = \varepsilon - Ir$. With no current, $V = \varepsilon$. The more current you draw, the more voltage is lost inside, and the battery warms up.
$$I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r}, \qquad V_{\text{terminal}} = \varepsilon - Ir = IR$$ The terminal voltage equals the EMF only when no current flows.

blocks.html: Circuits often combine several capacitors. The rules look like the ones for resistors, but switched: the series rule for capacitors is the parallel rule for resistors, and the other way around.

In parallel, each capacitor has the same voltage and their charges add: $Q = C_1V + C_2V$, so $C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2$. It is like making the plates bigger. In series, the inner plates are connected only to each other, so the charge they hold is pulled across from one to the other: every capacitor carries the same charge $Q$. Their voltages add: $V = \dfrac{Q}{C_1} + \dfrac{Q}{C_2}$, so $\dfrac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2}$. It is like making the gap wider.

Parallel: $C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots$ (same $V$, charges add). Series: $\dfrac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \cdots$ (same $Q$, voltages add), smaller than any one of them.

blocks.html: Put a resistor and a capacitor in a loop with a battery and the current changes with time: large at first, then fading away as the capacitor fills. The loop rule explains it, and the answer is the exponential decay you know from algebra, with the capacitance setting the clock.

The loop rule says $\varepsilon = IR + \dfrac{q}{C}$ at every moment. At the start $q = 0$, so $I = \varepsilon/R$: the empty capacitor acts like a plain wire. As charge builds, the capacitor's voltage $q/C$ pushes back, so less voltage is left for the resistor and the current drops. The charging rate is proportional to how far the capacitor still has to go, so the gap shrinks by the same fraction in each equal time: exponential decay, with time constant $\tau = RC$.

$\tau = RC$. Charging: $V_C = \varepsilon\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)$, $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}e^{-t/RC}$. Discharging: $V_C = V_0e^{-t/RC}$. At $t = 0$ an empty capacitor acts like a wire; after many $\tau$ a full capacitor blocks steady current.

blocks.html: In Electromagnets and Motors you saw that a current in a coil makes a magnet. That is the whole story of magnetism in one line: moving charge makes magnetic fields. A bar magnet works the same way. Its electrons spin and orbit, and in iron those tiny currents line up.

A magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is a vector at every point in space. A compass needle is a tiny magnet, and its north end points along $\vec{B}$. Field lines follow the compass: they leave a magnet's north pole and enter its south pole. Where the lines crowd together, the field is strong.

blocks.html: Magnetic field lines are closed loops. Outside a magnet they run from N to S; inside they run from S back to N. The field is measured in teslas: $1\ \text{T} = 1\ \text{N/(A·m)}$.

Electric field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones, because charges exist on their own. No one has ever found a magnetic "charge", a lone north or south pole. Every magnetic field comes from moving charge, and the field of a small current loop curls around and closes on itself. Add up loops and you still get closed lines. That is why cutting a magnet never isolates a pole: each piece is a complete magnet.

Thinking that field lines begin on the north pole and end on the south pole, like electric field lines on charges. Inside the magnet the lines keep going, from S to N, so every line is a loop. Check: a line that "ends" would need a magnetic charge there, and none has ever been found.

blocks.html: A magnetic field pushes on a charge only while the charge moves, and only on the part of its motion that cuts across the field. This is the magnetic partner of the electric force you met in The Electric Field, acting in the magnetic fields you have just met, and you will need vector components to split a velocity into parts along and across $\vec{B}$.

A charge $q$ moving at speed $v$ at angle $\theta$ to a field $B$ feels $$F = |q|\,vB\sin\theta.$$ The force points at right angles to both $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$. For a positive charge, use the right-hand rule; for a negative charge, the force points the other way.

blocks.html: This rule is how the field is defined: $B$ is the force per unit charge per unit speed, $B = F/(qv)$ for motion straight across the field. That gives the tesla its size, $1\ \text{T} = 1\ \text{N·s/(C·m)}$. The $\sin\theta$ says that only the part of the velocity across the field, $v\sin\theta$, counts. Motion along the field lines feels nothing.

Two common slips. (1) Thinking the force points along the field lines, as an electric force does. It never does: it is always sideways to $\vec{B}$. (2) Thinking a magnet pushes on a charge at rest. With $v = 0$ there is no magnetic force at all. Check: if your answer has $\vec{F}$ parallel to $\vec{B}$, or a force on a resting charge, start over.

blocks.html: In Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge you found that the magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity. In Forces in Circular Motion you met a force like that before: a sideways pull that bends a path into a circle without changing the speed.

A force at right angles to the motion does no work, $W = Fd\cos 90^\circ = 0$, so the kinetic energy and the speed never change. The force only turns the velocity. A constant-size force that keeps turning with the velocity is a centripetal force, so the charge moves in a circle: $$|q|vB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = \frac{mv}{|q|B}.$$
A charge moving across a uniform field circles at constant speed with radius and period $$r = \frac{mv}{|q|B}, \qquad T = \frac{2\pi m}{|q|B}.$$ The period does not depend on the speed.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: Switch the charge's sign and change its speed. A faster charge makes a bigger circle, but it takes the same time to go around.

blocks.html: Why is the period fixed? The time for one lap is $T = 2\pi r/v$. Put in $r = mv/(|q|B)$ and the $v$ cancels. A faster particle runs a longer lap at a higher speed. Cyclotrons use this: they kick particles in step with a period that never changes.

Thinking the magnetic force speeds the particle up as it circles. It cannot: it is always at right angles to the motion, so it does no work. Check: the kinetic energy at the end must equal the kinetic energy at the start. Only an electric field can change a charge's speed.

If the velocity has a part along $\vec{B}$, that part is untouched, and the circle stretches into a helix that winds along the field lines. That winding is how magnetic "bottles" hold hot plasma for fusion: try it in the Magnetic Bottles lab.

blocks.html: A current is a stream of moving charges (Electric Current), and each moving charge feels a magnetic force (Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge). Add up all those small pushes in a wire and you get a force on the wire itself. Every electric motor and loudspeaker runs on it.

Take a straight piece of wire of length $L$ carrying current $I$ across a field $B$. If the charges drift at speed $v_d$, it takes them a time $t = L/v_d$ to cross the piece, so the moving charge inside it is $Q = It = IL/v_d$. Each bit feels $qv_dB$, so the total is $$F = Qv_dB = \frac{IL}{v_d}\,v_dB = ILB.$$ The drift speed cancels. At an angle, only the part across the field counts, which brings back $\sin\theta$.

A straight wire of length $L$ carrying current $I$ at angle $\theta$ to a uniform field feels $$F = ILB\sin\theta,$$ at right angles to both the wire and the field. Point your fingers along the conventional current and curl them toward $\vec{B}$; your thumb gives $\vec{F}$.

blocks.html: So far the field came from somewhere else. Now we look at the field a current makes. In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed a compass needle swing when a wire nearby carried current. A long straight wire makes field lines that are circles around it, and the field gets weaker the farther you go. You already know the force on a current; put the two together and two wires push or pull on each other.

A long straight wire makes circles of field (thumb along $I$, fingers curl along $\vec{B}$): $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}.$$ Inside a long solenoid with $n$ turns per meter the field is nearly uniform: $$B = \mu_0 nI.$$ Two parallel wires a distance $d$ apart push or pull with $$\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d},$$ and same-direction currents attract.

Here $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T·m/A}$ (it is now measured, and it agrees with $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ to better than a part in a billion). A handy form: $$\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T·m/A}.$$

blocks.html: Why do parallel currents attract? Wire 1 makes a field at wire 2. Use the wire rule: with both currents up the page and wire 2 to the right, wire 1's field at wire 2 points into the page. Now the force rule on wire 2: fingers up (its current), curl into the page, and the thumb points left, toward wire 1. Reverse one current and the force reverses too. The rule for charges (like repel) does not carry over, because this is a different force.

Expecting parallel currents to repel, the way like charges do. Check with the two right-hand rules above: same-direction currents always come out attracting. This is how the ampere used to be defined: two wires $1\ \text{m}$ apart with $1\ \text{A}$ each pull with $2 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{N}$ per meter.

blocks.html: Faraday's discovery, coming up next, depends on one quantity: how much magnetic field passes through a loop of wire. That amount is the magnetic flux. It uses the cosine from Sine, Cosine and Tangent and the field you met in Magnetic Fields and Their Sources.

For a flat loop of area $A$ in a uniform field $B$, $$\Phi = BA\cos\theta,$$ where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{B}$ and the loop's normal (the line sticking straight out of the loop). The unit is the weber: $1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T·m}^2$.

Think of field lines as rain and the loop as a hoop. Held flat under the rain, the hoop catches the most. Tilted, it catches less, because the area it shows to the rain shrinks to $A\cos\theta$. Held edge-on, it catches none. The flux counts field lines the same way: $B$ times the area facing the field.

blocks.cap: Tilt the loop. The flux is largest at $\theta = 0$, when the field passes straight through, and zero at $90^\circ$, when the loop lies along the field.

If a problem says "the field makes $30^\circ$ with the plane of the loop", the angle from the normal is $90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$. blocks.html: In Generators and Induction you saw that moving a magnet near a coil makes a current. Faraday found the rule behind it in 1831, and it runs every generator and transformer. It is stated in terms of Magnetic Flux.

A changing magnetic flux through a coil of $N$ turns makes an emf $$\varepsilon = -N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}.$$ The size is $N|\Delta\Phi|/\Delta t$. The minus sign is Lenz's law, which sets the direction (the next topic). A steady flux, however large, makes no emf.

items: Change the field: push a magnet in, or turn up an electromagnet.
Change the area: squash the loop or slide a rod along rails.
Change the angle: turn the loop, as a generator does.

blocks.cap: The meter swings only while the flux changes. With the magnet resting inside the coil, the flux is large but steady, and the emf is zero.

blocks.html: Why the rate of change? An emf is energy per charge. Pushing a magnet in faster does the same change in less time, so the same work is done more quickly on the charges: a bigger emf for a shorter time. The emf times the time, $\varepsilon\,\Delta t = -N\Delta\Phi$, depends only on how much the flux changed.

Thinking a strong but steady field makes an emf. A magnet sitting still inside a coil makes no current at all. Only a change in flux counts. Check: if nothing in $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ is changing, the answer is $0\ \text{V}$.

blocks.html: Faraday's Law tells you how big the emf is. Lenz's law tells you which way the induced current flows. You will need the right-hand rule for loops from Fields of Wires and Solenoids: curl your fingers along the current and your thumb points along the field it makes inside the loop.

The induced current flows so that its own field opposes the change in flux. If the flux through a loop is growing, the induced field points against it. If the flux is shrinking, the induced field points the same way, trying to keep it.

items: Which way does the outside field point through the loop?
Is the flux through the loop growing or shrinking?
Growing: the induced field points the opposite way. Shrinking: the induced field points the same way.

blocks.html: Suppose the induced current helped the change instead. Push a magnet toward a coil, and the coil would pull it in faster, which would make more current, which would pull harder: energy from nothing. Opposing the change is what energy conservation demands. You do work pushing the magnet against the coil's push, and that work becomes the electrical energy.

Thinking the induced field always points against the magnet's field. It opposes the change. When a magnet is pulled away and the flux drops, the induced field points the same way as the magnet's field, trying to keep the flux up. Check: ask "growing or shrinking?" before anything else.

Pulling the magnet away makes that flux shrink.
To keep it, the induced field points the same way: to the right, away from you.
Thumb pointing away from you: your fingers curl clockwise, as you see it.

blocks.html: A metal rod sliding along two rails makes a loop whose area grows as the rod moves. By Faraday's Law, that growing flux makes an emf. And because a current then flows in the rod, the force on a current acts on the rod too.

Let the rails be $L$ apart and the rod move at speed $v$ in a field $B$ at right angles to the loop. In a time $\Delta t$ the rod moves $v\Delta t$, so the area grows by $\Delta A = Lv\Delta t$ and the flux by $B\,Lv\Delta t$. Faraday's law gives $$\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = BLv.$$ The same answer comes from the charges in the rod: each moves at $v$ through $B$, so each is pushed along the rod with force $qvB$. Over the length $L$ that is $qvBL$ of work per charge $q$, an emf of $BLv$.

A rod of length $L$ moving at speed $v$ across a field $B$ has an emf $\varepsilon = BLv$. With a circuit of resistance $R$, the current is $I = BLv/R$, and the field pushes on that current with $F = ILB$, always against the motion.

blocks.name: ph-induction
blocks.cap: Give the rod a push and let go. The magnetic force on the induced current points backward, so the rod slows down.

blocks.html: Forgetting the force on the induced current. That force always opposes the rod's motion (Lenz's law again), so to keep the rod moving at constant speed you must keep pushing with a force equal to $ILB$. Check with energy: your power $Fv$ must equal the electrical power $I^{2}R$. If the force helped the motion, the rod would speed up and make energy from nothing.

On the right side of a counterclockwise loop, the current runs toward the top of the page.

blocks.html: In Reflection, Absorption and Transmission you saw that light can bounce off a surface. Now we make that exact. In geometric optics we draw light as rays, straight lines along which the light travels, and we measure every angle from the normal, the line at right angles to the surface.

Law of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, $\theta_r = \theta_i$, both measured from the normal. A plane mirror makes a virtual, upright image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Why is the image behind the mirror? Rays from a point on the object bounce off with equal angles, so after reflecting they spread out exactly as if they came from a point behind the glass. Equal angles make two congruent triangles, which puts that point the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front. Your eye traces the rays straight back and sees the object there. No light actually reaches that point, so the image is virtual.

blocks.html: Light travels at $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$ in empty space, and slower in glass, water or plastic. In Refraction and Lenses you saw that this change of speed is why light bends. The ratio that measures the slowdown is the index of refraction. It ties to v = fλ, so a change in speed must change something else as well.
$$n = \frac{c}{v}, \qquad v = \frac{c}{n}, \qquad \lambda_{n} = \frac{\lambda}{n}.$$ In a material light is slower and its wavelength is shorter by the factor $n$, but its frequency stays the same.

head: Material
$n$ (yellow light)
blocks.cap: Light in a material is never faster than $c$, so $n \ge 1$. Air is so close to 1 that we use $n = 1.00$.

blocks.html: Why can't the frequency change? Picture crests reaching the surface of the glass. Each crest that arrives becomes a crest inside. If 500 trillion crests arrive per second but fewer left the surface each second, they would pile up there, and if more left, they would come from nowhere. So crests leave at the same rate they arrive. The frequency is fixed by the source; only the speed and the spacing change.

blocks.html: When light crosses into a material with a different index of refraction at an angle, it bends. Snell's law gives the exact angle. You will undo a sine with inverse trig to find it.

$$n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2 \sin\theta_2,$$ with both angles measured from the normal. Going into a higher index, light bends toward the normal; going into a lower index, it bends away. Light that hits head-on ($\theta_1 = 0$) goes straight through.

Picture a row of marchers crossing from pavement into mud at a slant. The end that reaches the mud first slows down first, so the row swings around. Light's wavefronts do the same. In one period, the wavefront moves $\lambda_1$ in material 1 and $\lambda_2$ in material 2, and the two pieces share the same stretch $s$ of the boundary: $\lambda_1 = s\sin\theta_1$ and $\lambda_2 = s\sin\theta_2$. Divide: $\dfrac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin\theta_2} = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$, which is Snell's law.

blocks.html: Snell's Law says that light going into a lower index bends away from the normal. Tilt the ray more and more, and the refracted ray swings toward the surface. At one angle it skims right along the surface. Beyond that, there is no refracted ray at all.

Going from a higher index $n_1$ to a lower index $n_2$, light at more than the critical angle $$\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$$ is totally reflected. It cannot happen going from a lower index into a higher one.

At the critical angle the refracted ray runs along the surface, $\theta_2 = 90^\circ$. Snell's law gives $n_1\sin\theta_c = n_2\sin 90^\circ = n_2$. For a bigger angle, Snell's law would need $\sin\theta_2 > 1$, which no angle has, so no light gets out: it all reflects. Going into a higher index, $\sin\theta_2 = \frac{n_1}{n_2}\sin\theta_1$ is always less than 1, so a refracted ray always exists.

blocks.html: A plane mirror (Reflection and Plane Mirrors) keeps rays spreading exactly as they were. A curved mirror bends their paths. A concave mirror, curved in like a cave or a spoon's bowl, gathers rays that arrive parallel to its axis to one point, the focal point $F$. A convex mirror, bulging out, spreads them as if they came from a focal point behind it. For a spherical mirror, $f = R/2$, half the radius of curvature.

Three principal rays from the tip of the object find the image: (1) a ray parallel to the axis reflects through $F$; (2) a ray through $F$ reflects parallel to the axis; (3) a ray through the center of curvature $C$ reflects straight back. Where the reflected rays meet is a real image; where they only seem to come from is a virtual image.

blocks.html: Ray diagrams show where an image is. The mirror equation says exactly where, and it is a rational equation you solve by working with reciprocals.

$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}, \qquad m = -\frac{d_i}{d_o} = \frac{h_i}{h_o}.$$ Signs: real is positive. $d_o > 0$ for a real object; $d_i > 0$ for a real image (in front of the mirror) and $d_i < 0$ for a virtual one (behind); $f > 0$ for concave and $f < 0$ for convex. $m < 0$ means inverted.

Draw the ray that hits the center of the mirror: it reflects at equal angles, making two similar triangles, so $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}$ (the minus because the image is inverted). The parallel ray reflects through $F$ and makes two more similar triangles: $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{d_i - f}{f}$. Set the two equal, $\frac{d_i}{d_o} = \frac{d_i - f}{f}$, and divide through by $d_i$: $\frac{1}{d_o} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{d_i}$. That is the mirror equation.

blocks.html: A lens bends light twice, once at each surface, by Snell's Law. A converging lens is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays together at a focal point on the far side. A diverging lens is thinner in the middle and spreads parallel rays as if they came from a focal point on the near side. Ray diagrams work just as for mirrors, but the light goes through.

Why does a thick-middled lens converge light? Near its edge, a lens is like a thin prism with its thick end toward the middle. A prism bends light toward its thicker part, so every part of the lens bends light toward the axis, and the edges, which are more steeply tilted, bend it most. That is just what it takes to bring parallel rays to one point.

Principal rays for a lens: (1) parallel to the axis, then through the far focal point (converging) or as if from the near one (diverging); (2) straight through the center, undeflected; (3) through the near focal point (converging) or aimed at the far one (diverging), then out parallel. Real images form on the far side of the lens.

blocks.html: The The Mirror Equation works for thin lenses too, with one change in where things are. For a lens, a real image forms on the far side, where the light goes, so that is where $d_i > 0$. Everything else, including the magnification, carries over from Lenses and Ray Diagrams.

$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}, \qquad m = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}.$$ $f > 0$ for a converging lens, $f < 0$ for a diverging lens. $d_i > 0$: real image on the far side. $d_i < 0$: virtual image on the object's side.

The same similar triangles as for a mirror appear. The ray through the center goes straight, so the object and image tips line up through the center: $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}$. The parallel ray bends through $F$, giving $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{d_i - f}{f}$. Setting them equal gives the same equation. The geometry is a mirror unfolded.

blocks.html: You know v = fλ. That equation links three quantities, but it does not say which one is in charge. The answer: the medium sets the speed, the source sets the frequency, and the wavelength is whatever fits, $\lambda = v/f$.
On a stretched string with tension $F_T$ and mass per length $\mu = m/L$, $$v = \sqrt{\frac{F_T}{\mu}}.$$ Shaking faster raises $f$ and shortens $\lambda$, but leaves $v$ alone.

A wave moves because each bit of string pulls on the next. Tension is the pull that snaps a displaced bit back, so more tension means a quicker response and a faster wave. Mass per length is the inertia that resists being moved, so a heavier string is slower. The square root comes from the units: $\frac{\text{N}}{\text{kg/m}} = \frac{\text{kg·m/s}^2}{\text{kg/m}} = \frac{\text{m}^2}{\text{s}^2}$, and only its square root is a speed. You found tension in Connected Objects and Tension; here it sets the speed.

blocks.html: Sound follows the same rule: stiffness against inertia. It travels about $343\ \text{m/s}$ in air at $20^\circ\text{C}$, roughly $1500\ \text{m/s}$ in water and several thousand meters per second in steel.

blocks.html: A wave changes in both space and time, but a graph has only one horizontal axis. So there are two kinds of wave graph, and reading the wrong one is a classic mistake. Both are pictures of the same wave.

A snapshot graph ($y$ against $x$) shows the whole wave at one instant: read the wavelength $\lambda$ between crests. A history graph ($y$ against $t$) follows one point over time: read the period $T$ between crests. Both show the amplitude $A$. Then $v = \lambda/T = f\lambda$.

blocks.name: ph-wave

opts.task: Find the wavelength on one graph and the period on the other.

blocks.cap: The snapshot graph freezes time; the history graph freezes position and watches the marked point bob up and down.

blocks.html: Why does the history graph look like a backward copy of the snapshot? For a wave moving to the right, the part of the wave just to the left of a point is what arrives there next. So the point's future displacements are the wave shape read from right to left. The two graphs have the same shape but different axes, with distance on one and time on the other, linked by $x = vt$.

Reading the "wavelength" off a $y$–$t$ graph. The distance between crests on a history graph is a time, the period $T$, measured in seconds. Check the axis label and the units: meters means wavelength, seconds means period.

blocks.html: A wave on a string travels at a speed set by the string. What happens when it reaches the end, or a knot joining a different string? Part of it bounces back, and how it bounces depends on the boundary.

A pulse reflects upside down from a fixed end (or from a heavier, slower string) and right side up from a free end (or from a lighter, faster string). At a junction, part of the pulse also passes through, always right side up, at the new speed. The frequency never changes at a boundary.

blocks.html: At a fixed end, the arriving pulse pulls up on the wall. By Newton's third law the wall pulls down on the string, and that downward pull launches an upside-down pulse back. At a free end (a ring sliding on a pole), nothing holds the end, so it swings up even higher and launches an upright pulse. A heavier string acts partly like a wall; a lighter one acts partly like a free end.

Thinking a reflected pulse always comes back the same way up, like a ball bouncing off a wall. A pulse is a shape moving along a string, not an object. Check: at a fixed end the end itself never moves, which only works if the incoming and reflected pulses cancel there, so the reflected one must be inverted.

blocks.title: A pulse round trip
blocks.q: A pulse moves at $40\ \text{m/s}$ on a $6.0\ \text{m}$ string tied to a wall. It starts upright at your hand. How long until it gets back to you, and which way up is it?
steps: It travels to the wall and back: $2 \times 6.0 = 12\ \text{m}$.
The wall is a fixed end, so the pulse comes back upside down.

blocks.title: Into a heavier string
blocks.q: A pulse $20\ \text{cm}$ wide moves at $30\ \text{m/s}$ on a light string tied to a heavier string, where waves move at $15\ \text{m/s}$. Describe the reflected and transmitted pulses.
steps: Reflected: a heavier string acts partly like a wall, so the reflected pulse is upside down, still $30\ \text{m/s}$ and $20\ \text{cm}$ wide.
Transmitted: right side up, moving at $15\ \text{m/s}$.
The front of the pulse crosses the knot first and slows down, so the back catches up: the width shrinks in proportion to the speed, $20 \times \frac{15}{30} = 10\ \text{cm}$.
blocks.a: Reflected inverted and $20\ \text{cm}$ wide; transmitted upright, $10\ \text{cm}$ wide

blocks.html: Light does the same thing. Reflecting off a material with a higher index of refraction, where light is slower, flips the wave over. That flip is the key to thin-film colors later in this unit.

blocks.html: In The Electromagnetic Spectrum you met the family of light, from radio to gamma rays. Now we can say what light is. Faraday's Law says a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell found the partner: a changing electric field makes a magnetic field. Each one keeps making the other, and the pair travels away as a wave.

An electromagnetic wave is linked electric and magnetic fields, at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, rising and falling together, with $E = cB$. In a vacuum every EM wave moves at $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$, and $c = f\lambda$. No medium is needed.

blocks.name: ph-wave
blocks.cap: The electric field (in one plane) and the magnetic field (in the plane at right angles) peak together as the wave moves.

blocks.html: Maxwell computed the speed of such a wave from two constants measured on lab benches with charges and currents, $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$, and got the measured speed of light. That match was the clue that light is an electromagnetic wave. Any accelerating charge makes these waves: electrons sloshing in a radio antenna, or jumping in an atom. The wave's electric part is the same kind of field as in The Electric Field: it pushes on charges, which is how a receiving antenna picks up the signal.

Two common mix-ups. (1) Thinking EM waves need a medium. Sunlight crosses $150$ million km of nearly empty space. (2) Thinking radio waves are a kind of sound. Sound is a pressure wave in matter at about $343\ \text{m/s}$; radio is light at $3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$. A radio turns the radio wave into sound with its speaker.

blocks.html: The electric field of an electromagnetic wave wiggles across the direction of travel. The direction it wiggles in is the wave's polarization. Light from the Sun or a bulb is unpolarized: a jumble of all directions. Only transverse waves have such a direction, which is the same sideways wiggle you saw on strings in Reflection at Boundaries. A polarizing filter passes only the part of the field along its axis.

Unpolarized light through a polarizer: $I = \frac{1}{2}I_0$. Polarized light through a polarizer at angle $\theta$ to its polarization (Malus's law): $$I = I_0\cos^{2}\theta.$$ Only transverse waves can be polarized.

A polarizer passes the component of $\vec{E}$ along its axis, $E\cos\theta$. Intensity goes as the field squared, so the intensity drops by $\cos^{2}\theta$. For unpolarized light, the angle takes every value; the average of $\cos^{2}\theta$ over all angles is $\frac{1}{2}$. Sound in air is a longitudinal wave, wiggling along its direction of travel, so there is no sideways direction for a filter to pick: it cannot be polarized.

blocks.html: When two waves meet in the same medium, what happens? With the wave graphs you can follow it point by point: the displacements simply add.

Superposition: where waves overlap, the total displacement is the sum of the separate displacements. Crest on crest builds up (constructive interference); crest on trough cancels (destructive interference). Afterward, each wave goes on unchanged.

blocks.name: ph-wave

opts.task: Step through the moment the pulses overlap. Then keep going: are they changed?

blocks.cap: Two pulses (dashed) and their sum (solid). They pass through each other and come out as they went in.

blocks.html: Why add? For small displacements, the force restoring each bit of string is proportional to how far it is displaced, so the equation of motion is linear: if each wave alone is a solution, their sum is a solution too. Nothing in the medium "remembers" which wave a bit of motion came from. Noise-canceling headphones use this: a microphone picks up the noise, and the speaker adds a copy turned upside down, so crest meets trough at your ear.

Thinking two waves that cancel are destroyed. At the instant two opposite pulses overlap exactly, the string is flat, but it is moving fast: the energy is all kinetic for that moment. A moment later both pulses re-emerge, unchanged. Check: energy cannot vanish, so the waves must still be there.

blocks.html: Waves on a guitar string reflect from both fixed ends (Reflection at Boundaries), so waves run both ways at once. By Superposition and Interference they add, and for certain frequencies the result stands still in place: a standing wave.

A string of length $L$ fixed at both ends resonates when a whole number of half-wavelengths fit: $$\lambda_n = \frac{2L}{n}, \qquad f_n = \frac{nv}{2L} = nf_1, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$ Nodes never move; antinodes swing the most. Neighboring nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart.

blocks.cap: The third harmonic: three loops, four nodes (counting the ends) and three antinodes.

blocks.html: Both ends are fixed, so both must be nodes. Nodes come every half wavelength, so the string must hold a whole number of half wavelengths, $L = n\frac{\lambda}{2}$. The wave speed is set by the string, $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$, so $f = v/\lambda = nv/(2L)$. Tighten the string and every note goes up; press a fret to shorten it and the pitch rises too. The lowest mode, $n = 1$, is the fundamental; the higher ones are harmonics, and the mix of harmonics a string plays at once gives each instrument its own sound.
Thinking a node is where the string moves the most. A node is a point that does not move at all; an antinode is where the string swings widest. Check: the fixed ends are nodes, and they never move.

blocks.html: Flutes, organ pipes and clarinets make music with standing sound waves in air columns. The idea is the same as for strings, but the ends work differently. As in Sound: Pitch and Loudness, sound is air moving back and forth along the pipe.

Open at both ends (all harmonics): $$f_n = \frac{nv}{2L}, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$ Closed at one end (odd harmonics only): $$f_n = \frac{nv}{4L}, \quad n = 1, 3, 5, \dots$$ A closed end is a displacement node; an open end is a displacement antinode.

blocks.html: Air can't move through a closed end, so it is a node. At an open end the air moves freely, so it is an antinode.
