blocks.html: In Sound: Pitch and Loudness, loudness came from amplitude. Physics measures it as intensity, power per area. Your ears handle a range of intensities of about a trillion to one, so we squeeze that range with What a Logarithm Is.

A source of power $P$ spreading in all directions gives $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^{2}}$ at distance $r$. The sound level is $$\beta = 10\log_{10}\frac{I}{I_0}\ \text{dB}, \qquad I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2.$$ Every $+10\ \text{dB}$ means $10$ times the intensity; $+3\ \text{dB}$ is about double.

The power spreads over a sphere of area $4\pi r^{2}$, so twice as far means four times the area and a quarter of the intensity. For decibels: $\log_{10}$ turns multiplying into adding. Multiply $I$ by 10 and $\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ goes up by 1, so $\beta$ goes up by 10. Multiply by 2 and $\beta$ goes up by $10\log_{10}2 = 3.0\ \text{dB}$. $I_0$ is roughly the faintest sound a young ear can hear, so $0\ \text{dB}$ is the threshold of hearing, not silence.

Thinking that doubling the intensity doubles the decibel level. Two identical $60\ \text{dB}$ speakers give $63\ \text{dB}$, not $120\ \text{dB}$. Check: $120\ \text{dB}$ is a million times $60\ \text{dB}$ in intensity, far more than two speakers can add.

blocks.html: An ambulance siren sounds higher as it comes toward you and lower as it goes away. The siren never changes; the waves reaching you do. The speed of sound is set by the air (What Sets a Wave's Speed), so motion changes the spacing of the crests you receive. As in Sound: Pitch and Loudness, the frequency you hear is the pitch.

$$f' = f\,\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$$ Use the upper signs when source and observer move toward each other, the lower signs when they move apart. Here $v$ is the speed of sound, $v_o$ the observer's speed and $v_s$ the source's. Approaching raises the pitch.

blocks.name: ph-doppler

opts.task: Compare the spacing of the wavefronts ahead of the source and behind it.

blocks.cap: A moving source. Crests bunch up ahead and spread out behind, so the observer ahead hears a higher pitch.

blocks.html: A source with frequency $f$ sends a crest every $T = 1/f$. If it moves toward you at $v_s$, each crest starts $v_sT$ closer than the one before, so the crests arrive $\lambda' = (v - v_s)T$ apart. They still move at $v$, so you hear $f' = \frac{v}{\lambda'} = f\frac{v}{v - v_s}$. A moving observer meets crests more often: $f' = f\frac{v + v_o}{v}$.

Thinking the pitch keeps rising as an approaching source gets closer. At constant speed the higher pitch is steady; it drops suddenly to a lower steady pitch as the source passes you. Check with the formula: nothing in it depends on the distance.

blocks.html: Light does the same. Light from a galaxy moving away arrives with longer wavelengths (redshift), which is how astronomers measure the motions of stars and galaxies.

blocks.html: Waves spread out as they pass through an opening or around an edge. That spreading is diffraction. You can hear someone around a corner because sound waves, about a meter long, bend around doorways. Light waves are a million times shorter, so light's diffraction only shows through very narrow openings. The dark bands it makes come from Superposition and Interference, and the angles come from Sine, Cosine and Tangent.

Light of wavelength $\lambda$ through a slit of width $a$ makes dark fringes at $$a\sin\theta = m\lambda, \quad m = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$$ The central bright band runs between the two first dark fringes; on a screen a distance $L$ away it is about $2\lambda L/a$ wide (small angles). A narrower slit makes a wider pattern.

blocks.name: ph-interference

opts.task: Make the slit narrower. Does the central band get narrower or wider?

blocks.cap: A single slit and the pattern on a far screen: a wide central band with dim bands on each side.

blocks.html: Split the slit into a top half and a bottom half. Pair each point in the top half with the point $a/2$ below it. At the angle where those two are half a wavelength out of step, $\frac{a}{2}\sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2}$, every pair cancels and the screen is dark. That is $a\sin\theta = \lambda$. A narrow slit needs a bigger angle to make that half-wave difference, so the pattern spreads.

Thinking a narrower slit makes a narrower central bright band, as if the slit were a stencil. Diffraction works the other way: $\sin\theta = \lambda/a$ grows as $a$ shrinks. Check: shrink $a$ toward $\lambda$ and the central band spreads over the whole screen.

steps: Small angles: $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta = y/L$, so the first dark fringe is at $y = \dfrac{\lambda L}{a}$.
The band runs from $-y$ to $+y$: width $2y = 0.026\ \text{m} = 2.6\ \text{cm}$.

blocks.html: In 1801 Thomas Young sent light through two close slits and saw bright and dark stripes, proof that light is a wave. Each slit acts as a source, the two are in step, and the waves from them interfere. Where they arrive in step, the screen is bright.

For slits a distance $d$ apart, bright fringes appear where $$d\sin\theta = m\lambda, \quad m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$$ and dark ones where $d\sin\theta = (m + \frac{1}{2})\lambda$. For small angles on a screen at distance $L$: $y_m = \dfrac{m\lambda L}{d}$, so bright fringes are $\Delta y = \dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$ apart.

From a far point on the screen, the rays from the two slits are almost parallel, and the lower ray travels farther by the short side of a small right triangle: $d\sin\theta$ (sine of the angle times the hypotenuse $d$). A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths puts crest on crest. For small angles, $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta = y/L$, which gives $y = m\lambda L/d$.

opts.task: Move the slits closer together. Do the fringes squeeze together or spread apart?

blocks.cap: Two slits and their fringes. The fringe spacing is $\lambda L/d$.

blocks.html: Thinking that moving the slits closer together squeezes the fringes closer. It spreads them: $\Delta y = \lambda L/d$, so a smaller $d$ gives a bigger spacing. Check the extreme: as $d$ shrinks toward zero, the two slits become one source and the pattern spreads out into one wide blur.

blocks.html: A diffraction grating is thousands of evenly spaced slits. The rule for where the bright lines go is the same as for the Double-Slit Interference, but with so many slits the bright lines become very sharp and bright, and the space between them goes dark. That makes gratings the heart of spectrometers.

For a grating with $N$ lines per meter, the slit spacing is $d = \dfrac{1}{N}$, and bright lines appear at $$d\sin\theta = m\lambda.$$ Because $\sin\theta \le 1$, the highest order you can see is the largest whole number $m$ with $m\lambda \le d$.

blocks.name: ph-interference

opts.task: Raise the lines per millimeter. What happens to the angles?

blocks.cap: A grating's sharp bright lines. More lines per millimeter means a smaller $d$ and larger angles.

blocks.html: At an angle where neighboring slits are a whole wavelength apart, every slit is in step with every other one, so all of them add up: a bright line. Move a little off that angle and the slits get steadily out of step across the grating, and with thousands of them some slit always cancels another. So the bright lines are narrow. Different colors land at different angles, spreading white light into a spectrum.

Using the number of lines per millimeter as $d$. A grating marked "$600$ lines/mm" has $d = \frac{1}{600}\ \text{mm} = 1.67 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}$, not $600$ of anything. Check: $d$ is a small length, a few times the wavelength; if $\sin\theta$ comes out tiny or huge, you probably forgot the reciprocal.

blocks.html: The colors of a soap bubble or an oil slick come from light reflecting off the top and the bottom of a very thin layer. The two reflections interfere, like the two slits did. Two details decide which colors win: the wavelength inside the film is shorter (Index of Refraction), and a reflection can flip the wave (Reflection at Boundaries).

At nearly straight-on viewing, the ray from the bottom surface travels an extra $2t$ inside a film of thickness $t$, where the wavelength is $\lambda/n_{\text{film}}$. A reflection off a higher index adds a half-wave flip. One flip: bright when $2t = (m + \frac{1}{2})\frac{\lambda}{n}$. Zero or two flips: bright when $2t = m\frac{\lambda}{n}$. Dark is the other way around.

blocks.name: ph-interference

opts.task: Change the thickness and watch the reflected color change.

blocks.cap: Two reflected rays from a thin film. The flips are marked, and the color is what survives.

blocks.html: Count the delay in wavelengths. The extra path $2t$ inside the film is $2t\big/\frac{\lambda}{n}$ wavelengths. Each flip adds half a wavelength. If the two rays end up a whole number of wavelengths apart, they reinforce; a half number, they cancel. A soap film in air flips only the top reflection (air to soap is low to high; soap to air is high to low), so the conditions swap.

Two slips. (1) Forgetting that the wavelength inside the film is $\lambda/n$. (2) Missing a half-wave flip, or adding one where there is none. Check each surface separately: does the light go from lower $n$ to higher $n$? Then that reflection flips.

blocks.html: In Higher Frequency, More Energy you met the idea that light comes in packets. Here we put numbers on it. Light is an electromagnetic wave, but it delivers its energy in lumps called photons, and the size of each lump depends only on the frequency.

$$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}, \qquad h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J·s}.$$ In atomic units: $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ (the energy one electron gains crossing $1\ \text{V}$, as in Electric Potential and Voltage), and $hc = 1240\ \text{eV·nm}$, so $E\,(\text{eV}) = \dfrac{1240}{\lambda\,(\text{nm})}$.

blocks.name: ph-spectrum
blocks.cap: The spectrum with a photon-energy ruler: radio photons carry a millionth of an eV or less; X-ray photons carry thousands of eV.

blocks.html: Why is $hc = 1240\ \text{eV·nm}$ so handy? Work it once: $$\begin{aligned} hc &= (6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3.00 \times 10^{8}) \\ &= 1.988 \times 10^{-25}\ \text{J·m}. \end{aligned}$$ Divide by $1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J/eV}$ and multiply by $10^{9}\ \text{nm/m}$: $1240\ \text{eV·nm}$. Visible light, $400$ to $700\ \text{nm}$, comes out to $3.1$ to $1.8\ \text{eV}$ per photon, the same size as the energies of electrons in atoms and molecules. That is why light can drive chemistry and vision.

Thinking brighter light has more energetic photons. Brightness is how many photons arrive each second; the energy of each one is set by the color (frequency). A dim blue light has more energetic photons than a bright red one. Check: brightness appears nowhere in $E = hf$. That is why old photo darkrooms could use red lamps: a red photon carries too little energy to change the light-sensitive chemicals in photo paper, however many of them arrive.

blocks.html: Shine light on a clean metal and electrons can fly off. The wave picture of light predicted that any color would work if it were bright enough, and that dim light would need time to build up energy. Experiments said otherwise, and in 1905 Einstein explained why with Photons.

Each electron absorbs one photon. It escapes only if $hf$ exceeds the metal's work function $\phi$, and the fastest electrons leave with $$K_{\max} = hf - \phi.$$ The threshold frequency is $f_0 = \phi/h$ (threshold wavelength $\lambda_0 = hc/\phi$). The stopping voltage is $V_s = K_{\max}/e$.

blocks.name: ph-photon

opts.task: Make the light red and very bright. Do any electrons come out? Then try dim violet light.

blocks.cap: One photon, one electron. Below the threshold no electrons leave, however bright the light.

blocks.html: The work function is the least energy it takes to pull an electron free, like the cost of climbing out of a well. A photon hands over all its energy $hf$ at once. If $hf < \phi$, the electron falls back, and more photons don't help, since an electron essentially never gets two at once. If $hf > \phi$, the extra becomes kinetic energy. Brighter light means more photons, so more electrons, but each one still gets the same $hf$.

blocks.html: In Bright-Line Spectra you saw that each element glows in its own set of colors. In 1913 Niels Bohr explained hydrogen's colors: the electron can only have certain energies, and light comes out only when it drops from one to another, as a photon.

Hydrogen's allowed energies are $$E_n = -\frac{13.6\ \text{eV}}{n^{2}}, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$ A jump between levels emits or absorbs one photon with $E_{\text{photon}} = E_{\text{upper}} - E_{\text{lower}}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{1240\ \text{eV·nm}}{E_{\text{photon}}}$.

blocks.name: ph-spectrum

opts.task: Find the jump that gives the red line near 656 nm.

blocks.cap: Hydrogen's levels. Jumps down to $n = 1$ give ultraviolet light, to $n = 2$ visible light and to $n = 3$ infrared.

blocks.html: Why negative energies? Zero is set for an electron just barely free of the proton. A bound electron has less energy than that, so its energy is negative, and $13.6\ \text{eV}$ is what it takes to free it from the lowest level (the ionization energy). Bohr's rule that only certain orbits are allowed was later explained by the electron's wave nature: only orbits that fit whole numbers of its wavelength survive.

Two slips. (1) Thinking the electron gives off light the whole time it circles. In an allowed level it does not radiate; light comes only from a jump. (2) Counting only the jumps that end on $n = 1$. From $n = 4$ the electron can go to 3, 2 or 1, and from each of those down again: $4\to3$, $4\to2$, $4\to1$, $3\to2$, $3\to1$, $2\to1$, six lines in all. In general $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

blocks.title: The red line
blocks.q: Find the photon energy and wavelength for hydrogen's jump from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$.
steps: $\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{1.89} = 656\ \text{nm}$: red, the brightest line in hydrogen's visible spectrum.

blocks.title: Absorbing a photon
blocks.q: Hydrogen atoms in the ground state are hit by photons of $10.2\ \text{eV}$ and of $11.0\ \text{eV}$. Which are absorbed?
steps: From $n = 1$: $$E_2 - E_1 = -3.40 - (-13.6) = 10.2\ \text{eV}.$$ A $10.2\ \text{eV}$ photon fits exactly and is absorbed.
$E_3 - E_1 = 12.1\ \text{eV}$. $11.0\ \text{eV}$ matches no jump, and it is below the $13.6\ \text{eV}$ needed to ionize, so it passes by.
An atom takes whole photons only, and only at the exact energy of a jump.

blocks.html: The The Bohr Model and Energy Levels says each kind of atom has its own ladder of energy levels, so it emits and absorbs its own set of photon energies. That is how astronomers know what the stars are made of, without ever touching one.

Kirchhoff's three rules: a hot, dense object (a solid, or a dense gas like a star's interior) gives a continuous spectrum. A hot, thin gas gives an emission spectrum of bright lines. A cooler, thin gas in front of a hotter continuous source gives an absorption spectrum: dark lines at the same wavelengths that gas would emit.

blocks.name: ph-spectrum
blocks.cap: One lamp and one cloud of hydrogen gas. Straight through the gas you see dark lines; from the side you see the same lines bright.

blocks.html: Why the same lines? Both come from the same jumps. A photon is absorbed only if its energy matches a jump up, and an atom emits only the energies of jumps down, and the jumps up and down are between the same pairs of levels. Why are absorption lines dark? The atoms that absorb a photon soon re-emit one, but in a random direction, so very little of that light continues toward you.

Thinking a gas absorbs different colors from the ones it emits. The dark lines line up exactly with the bright lines of the same gas. (Which lines show up depends on which levels the atoms sit in: cool hydrogen, nearly all in $n = 1$, absorbs only its ultraviolet lines; in a hot star's atmosphere many atoms sit in $n = 2$, so the visible lines appear dark.) Check: every absorption line must match an emission line of that element.

blocks.title: Which spectrum?
blocks.q: You look at three things through a spectroscope: a glowing stove element, a neon sign, and sunlight. Which kind of spectrum does each give?
steps: Stove element: a hot solid, so a continuous spectrum.
Neon sign: a hot, thin gas, so bright emission lines.
Sunlight: the hot, dense Sun seen through its cooler outer layers, so a continuous spectrum crossed by dark absorption lines.

blocks.title: Counting lines
blocks.q: A gas has energy levels at $-10.0$, $-6.0$ and $-4.0\ \text{eV}$. List the photon energies it can emit. If all its atoms start in the lowest level, which can it absorb?
steps: Emission (any jump down): $-6.0 \to -10.0$ gives $4.0\ \text{eV}$; $-4.0 \to -10.0$ gives $6.0\ \text{eV}$; $-4.0 \to -6.0$ gives $2.0\ \text{eV}$.
Absorption from the lowest level: only jumps that start at $-10.0\ \text{eV}$: $4.0$ and $6.0\ \text{eV}$.
The $2.0\ \text{eV}$ line would need atoms already in the middle level.

blocks.html: In 1868 astronomers found a bright yellow line in the Sun's spectrum that matched no known element. The new element was named helium, from the Greek word for the Sun, and it was found on Earth 27 years later.

blocks.html: If light, a wave, comes in particles, could particles act like waves? In 1924 Louis de Broglie said yes, using the same link between momentum and wavelength that photons obey. You know momentum $p = mv$ from Linear Momentum; the Double-Slit Interference is the test.
Every particle has a wavelength $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}.$$ An electron accelerated from rest through a voltage $V$ has $p = \sqrt{2meV}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}$.

blocks.name: ph-interference

opts.task: Let the electrons land one at a time. When does the pattern appear?

blocks.cap: Electrons sent through two slits one at a time. Each lands as a dot, yet the dots build up a two-slit interference pattern.

blocks.html: Why don't we see a baseball diffract? Its wavelength is absurdly small. A $0.15\ \text{kg}$ ball at $40\ \text{m/s}$ has $\lambda = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{6.0} \approx 10^{-34}\ \text{m}$, far smaller than a proton. Waves show their wave nature only when they meet gaps or obstacles about their own size. An electron's wavelength is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, so crystals diffract electrons, as Davisson and Germer found in 1927. Electron microscopes use electrons whose wavelengths are far shorter than light's, so they can show details far too small for any light microscope.

Thinking only light can act like a wave. Electrons, neutrons, atoms and even large molecules have all been diffracted. Check the size: compare $\lambda = h/p$ with the gaps the particle passes through; when they are similar, expect wave behavior.

blocks.html: A photon has no mass, but it carries momentum. Turn the de Broglie relation around: a photon of wavelength $\lambda$ has $p = h/\lambda$. In 1923 Arthur Compton bounced X-rays off electrons and found that the photons behave like billiard balls in a collision, conserving both energy and momentum.

A photon has momentum $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{E}{c}$. A photon that scatters off a free electron at angle $\theta$ comes away with a longer wavelength: $$\Delta\lambda = \lambda' - \lambda = \frac{h}{m_e c}(1 - \cos\theta),$$ where $\dfrac{h}{m_e c} = 2.43\ \text{pm}$ (the Compton wavelength of the electron).

blocks.name: ph-photon

opts.task: Raise the scattering angle. When is the shift largest?

blocks.cap: An X-ray photon strikes an electron at rest. The electron recoils, and the photon leaves with less energy and a longer wavelength.

blocks.html: The electron recoils and carries off some kinetic energy. The photon must lose that much energy, and for a photon less energy means a lower frequency and a longer wavelength, since $E = hc/\lambda$. Its speed cannot change: every photon moves at $c$. A head-on bounce ($\theta = 180^\circ$) gives the electron the biggest kick, so the shift is largest there, $2(2.43) = 4.86\ \text{pm}$. A grazing scatter ($\theta \to 0$) changes almost nothing.

Thinking the scattered photon slows down. It still moves at $c$; its lost energy shows up as a longer wavelength (lower frequency). Check: the shift depends only on the angle, and $\lambda'$ is always longer than $\lambda$.

blocks.q: X-rays of $71.0\ \text{pm}$ scatter at $90^\circ$ from free electrons. Find the scattered wavelength.

blocks.q: For the same scattering, how much kinetic energy does the electron get? Use $hc = 1240\ \text{eV·nm} = 1.240 \times 10^{6}\ \text{eV·pm}$.
steps: The electron gets the difference: about $580\ \text{eV}$, so the photon gave up about $3\%$ of its energy.

blocks.html: In Fission and Fusion you saw that nuclear reactions release energy as a little mass disappears. Einstein's $E = mc^{2}$ says how much: mass is a form of energy, with $c^{2}$ as the exchange rate. Energy is conserved, as in Conservation of Mechanical Energy, once you count rest energy too. Nuclear energies are millions of times bigger than chemical ones, so we measure them in MeV: $1\ \text{MeV} = 10^{6}\ \text{eV}$, and an electron volt is the energy one electron gains crossing $1\ \text{V}$ (Electric Potential and Voltage).

$E = mc^{2}$. A nucleus has less mass than its separate protons and neutrons. The missing mass, the mass defect $\Delta m$, times $c^{2}$ is the binding energy, the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart. In atomic units, $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^{2}$.

When protons and neutrons snap together, the strong force pulls them into a deep energy well and the binding energy leaves as gamma rays and kinetic energy. The bound nucleus then has less total energy than the parts had apart, and since $E = mc^{2}$, less mass. To separate them again you must put that energy back. The more tightly bound, the bigger the mass defect per nucleon.

blocks.name: ph-nucleus
blocks.cap: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron and nickel. Fusing light nuclei or splitting heavy ones both move toward the peak, releasing energy.

blocks.html: Thinking a nucleus should weigh more than its parts because it "holds" energy. The binding energy was released when it formed, so the nucleus has less energy and less mass than its separate parts. Check: a nucleus that weighed more than its parts would fly apart on its own and give off energy.

blocks.q: In the fusion reaction $^{2}\text{H} + {}^{3}\text{H} \to {}^{4}\text{He} + n$, the masses are $2.014102$, $3.016049$, $4.002603$ and $1.008665\ \text{u}$. How much energy is released?
steps: $Q = (0.018883)(931.5) = 17.6\ \text{MeV}$, mostly carried off by the neutron.

blocks.title: Mass into joules
blocks.q: How much energy is $1.0\ \text{g}$ of mass?
steps: $E = 9.0 \times 10^{13}\ \text{J}$, roughly the energy of $20$ thousand tonnes of TNT.
